There is a version of the city that only appears between 3:07 and 3:19 in the morning. The streetlights hum at a different frequency then. The traffic signals, having no traffic to direct, blink yellow at one another like old men exchanging secrets. The bakeries are dark but not empty; you can smell the yeast dreaming. And on the night bus—the 47, which runs a loop from the river to the hill and back again—there is a driver named Marisol who has learned to recognize the regulars who are not quite ghosts.

She began keeping a notebook after the third Thursday. It was a small thing, blue cover, pencil stub tied to the spiral with kitchen string. She wrote down what she saw, not because she believed it, but because writing made the strangeness behave. A man in a raincoat who boarded at the cemetery gates and rode exactly four stops, always reading a book with blank pages. A teenager with silver headphones who stood even when every seat was empty. A woman carrying a potted fern that whispered when the bus turned corners. Marisol wrote: *The fern says “left.” It is usually correct.*

At first she thought she was just tired. Night shifts do strange things to the mind; they peel back the wallpaper. But then she noticed the bus itself had opinions. The fare box accepted coins that were not there. The back doors opened a half-second before she pressed the button. Once, on a night thick with fog, the route map above the driver’s seat rearranged itself, adding a street called Larkspur Lane that did not exist on any map she could find. The next day she drove past the place where it should have been, and there was only a vacant lot full of thistles and a shopping cart with one wheel missing. The night after that, Larkspur Lane was back on the map, and a woman with a red umbrella was waiting at its corner.

Marisol stopped the bus. The woman climbed on, folded her umbrella, and paid with a button. She sat in the third row and stared out the window as if the dark were a movie she had already seen. Marisol asked, in the way that bus drivers ask questions without turning around, “Where are you headed?”

“To the place where the light goes,” the woman said.

“Which light?”

“The one you lost.”

Marisol had not lost a light. She had a small lamp in her apartment that she kept on all day because she did not like coming home to darkness. She had a flashlight in the glove compartment of her car. She had a lighter in her pocket even though she did not smoke. But the woman’s voice made her think of something else—a memory of standing on a beach as a child, holding a sparkler, watching the bright needles dissolve into the wind. She had cried when it went out. Her father had said, *Everything ends, but not everything goes away.*

The bus continued. The fog leaned close. At the top of the hill, where the road usually curved right toward the reservoir, it curved left instead. Marisol did not turn the wheel. She watched her hands stay still. The bus moved as if on rails, down a street of houses with lit windows and no doors, past a playground where swings moved in a wind she could not feel, and finally to a small square with a fountain made of glass. In the fountain’s basin, coins glinted under water that was not wet.

The woman with the red umbrella stood. “Last stop,” she said.

“This isn’t the route,” Marisol said.

“It is tonight.”

Marisol did not know why she followed her off the bus. It was against every rule she had. But the woman walked to the fountain and reached into the water—if it was water—and pulled out a coin, dark with age. She handed it to Marisol. On one side was a bus, tiny and perfect, with its headlights on. On the other was a word Marisol could not read until she tilted it toward the streetlight. *Return.*

“What does it mean?” Marisol asked.

“It means you can go back,” the woman said. “Or not. The coin likes a decision.”

Marisol looked at the bus. Its doors were open. The interior light was warm and ordinary. She thought of her notebook, her small apartment, the lamp that stayed on all day. She thought of the route map with a street that did not exist and the fern that said *left* and the man who read a book of blank pages. She thought of how tired she was, and how being tired had made the world larger instead of smaller.

“I think I’ll keep the coin,” she said.

The woman smiled. “Most people do.”

When Marisol turned around, the square was gone. She was standing at the reservoir, the bus idling beside her, the engine ticking as if it had just been running. The fog was lifting. The sky above the hill was the color of an old bruise turning yellow. She climbed back into the driver’s seat and checked the rearview mirror. The bus was empty except for a single fern leaf on the floor, green and curled like a question mark.

She drove the rest of the route in silence. The fare box did not accept anything unusual. The doors opened when she pressed the button. At the end of the line, she parked, turned off the engine, and opened her notebook. She turned to a fresh page, wrote the date, and then sat for a long time with the pencil in her hand. Finally she wrote: *Tonight the city asked me a question. I am still deciding how to answer.*

Then she put the coin in her pocket, stepped off the bus, and walked home as the ordinary morning began to assemble itself around her—newspapers on doorsteps, dogs barking at nothing, the first bus of the day sighing at the corner, full of people who had never once been lost.
